ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text: As shown in the figure, within the circular region indicated by the dashed line there exists a uniform magnetic field perpendicular to the plane of the paper. P is a point on the boundary of the magnetic field. A large number of identical charged particles pass through point P with the same speed and enter the magnetic field in the plane of the paper along different directions. If the speed at which the particles enter is v1, the exit points of these particles on the boundary of the magnetic field are distributed over one-sixth of the circumference; if the speed at which the particles enter is v2, the corresponding exit points are distributed over one-third of the circumference. Neglecting gravity and the interactions between the charged particles, then v2:v1 is (　　)

ready2_open_rewrite.resolved_question_text: As shown in the figure, within the circular region indicated by the dashed line there exists a uniform magnetic field perpendicular to the plane of the paper, and P is a point on the boundary of the magnetic field. A large number of identical charged particles pass through point P with the same speed and enter the magnetic field in the plane of the paper along different directions. If the speed at which the particles enter is v1, the exit points of these particles on the boundary of the magnetic field are distributed over one-sixth of the circumference; if the speed at which the particles enter is v2, the corresponding exit points are distributed over one-third of the circumference. Neglecting gravity and the interactions between the charged particles, find v2:v1.
ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: First describe the image: In the figure there is a circular boundary drawn with a dashed line, indicating a circular magnetic-field region; point P is located at the left edge of the circular boundary; from point P there are multiple arrows pointing into the circle, indicating that identical charged particles enter the magnetic field at the same speed but along different directions. Then reason: Let the radius of the dashed circular magnetic-field boundary be R, and let the radius of the circular motion of the particles in the uniform magnetic field be r. For an exit point X on some boundary, the trajectory of the particle inside the magnetic field is a circular arc of radius r, and the circle on which this circular arc lies passes through P and X. The condition for such a circle to exist is that the chord length PX is not greater than the diameter of the motion circle, that is, PX≤2r. As the incident direction changes, all boundary points on one side that satisfy this condition may become exit points; the endpoints of the distribution of exit points correspond to PX=2r. If the proportion of the magnetic-field boundary circumference occupied by the exit-point distribution is f, then the corresponding central angle of the boundary is alpha=2πf. The longest chord length from P to an endpoint in this distributed arc segment is 2R sin(alpha/2). The endpoint satisfies 2R sin(alpha/2)=2r, so r=R sin(alpha/2). For charged particles in the same magnetic field, r=mv/(|q|B), so r is proportional to v. When the speed is v1, f1=1/6, alpha1=2π·1/6=π/3, r1=R sin(π/6)=R/2. When the speed is v2, f2=1/3, alpha2=2π·1/3=2π/3, r2=R sin(π/3)=√3 R/2. Therefore v2:v1=r2:r1=(√3 R/2):(R/2)=√3:1.
